newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Nuclear material disappears from Swedish airport.
newsitem.headline: Nuclear material disappears from Swedish airport.

text.p: Police at Stockholm's international airport said on Friday they had launched an investigation into the disappearance of more than one tonne of a type of radioactive material used in nuclear warheads.

Airport police inspector Ake Granberg at Arlanda airport told Reuters that Interpol and Swedish security police were involved in the search for 1,027.5 kg (2,260.5 pounds) of beryllium from an airport freight terminal almost one year ago.
A tip-off from a lorry driver prompted a search for the material, which was transferred through Arlanda airport after arriving at Stockholm from Tallinn in Estonia by boat.
"A lorry driver confirmed to me that he unloaded it at Arlanda in a freight terminal on December 29 (1995). I believe his story -- he has no motive not to tell the truth," Granberg said.
The material should have been prepared in the cargo terminal to be flown to the United States to its buyer, a New Jersey-based company, Granberg said.
Investigators did not know where the cargo had gone. "There is very little demand for beryllium in Sweden. I suspect it has been transported to another country," said Granberg.

Although other airport employees questioned said they did not see the shipment, one of the wooden pallets on which the shipment was loaded was later discovered in the terminal with traces of beryllium, he said.
According to an invoice the shipment, which was entirely legal, was valued at around $97,000, he said. Other sources said, however, the material could be worth a lot more.
The material was of high enough quality to be used in nuclear weapons but has commercial uses as well, Granberg said.

The beryllium was loaded in several barrels strapped to two pallets. In this form the metal was not dangerous but it could be hazardous to human health if people inhaled the beryllium dust or touched it.
Police were waiting for results of a police investigation into the U.S. company and the next step would be to look into the origin of the shipment, thought to come from Russia.
"I will do an investigation into the company that delivered the goods to Sweden," Granberg said.
The Baltic countries are suspected of being gateways for the smuggling to the West of radioactive and rare metals pilfered from the former Soviet bloc.
In May 1993, Lithuanian police seized four tonnes of radioactive beryllium in the basement of a Vilnius bank.
The investigative U.S. news programme "Sixty Minutes" later reported that the material was destined for a mystery buyer in Switzerland for a price of $24 million.
The programme said Russian and Lithuanian gangs of smugglers were behind the operation, which is blamed for the deaths of 10 people killed in connection with the shipment.
